title: Query Optimisation: Plan Space
lead: Identify equivalent execution plans before comparing their estimated costs.
goals: Distinguish the parser, rewriter, and cost-based optimizer
Describe query blocks and the System R approach
Apply logical equivalences and safe simplifications
Change join order while preserving predicates and handling cross products

sections.title: Three different optimization decisions
sections.html:
Query optimization must answer three questions: which plans are equivalent (the plan space), how much each plan is expected to cost (cost estimation), and how to explore the candidates (search). Parsing and semantic analysis check the query and produce an internal representation. A rewriter transforms the query while preserving its result. The cost-based optimizer uses statistics to compare execution choices. Search time is limited, and costs are estimates.

Original worked example: WHERE 2=3 is always false, so the system can produce an empty filtered input without scanning the data. Later operators must still be evaluated correctly: for example, COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row containing 0 for that empty input. WHERE amount>20 AND amount>50 can be simplified to amount>50. However, a join cannot be removed merely because the output uses no right-hand columns: multiple matches on the right can still increase the number of output rows.

Key takeaway

A correct rewrite must preserve each row’s multiplicity. Under SQL bag semantics, the same values with different numbers of copies constitute different results.

Related source material: PDF pages 1–3. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Equivalence must preserve columns and predicates
sections.html:
For the deterministic relational predicates considered here, two filter conditions connected by AND can be split into two selections and reordered. Projection can be pushed down if it retains every column needed by later filters, joins, and output operations. Inner joins can be reordered, but each predicate must be checked where all the columns it uses are available. For example, a condition using a column from S cannot be evaluated in a subtree containing only R and T.

Original worked example: consider Orders(customer_id,product_id), Customers(id,name,region), and Products(id,price). To find the names of customers who bought expensive products, Products can be filtered first. A projection on Orders must keep customer_id to join Customers and product_id to join Products. Forming Customers×Products first may still produce a correct final result if all predicates are subsequently applied, but it may generate a very large intermediate relation.

Related source material: PDF pages 4–4. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Heuristics are useful, but do not guarantee the fastest plan
sections.html:
Pushing filters down often reduces cardinality, which is the number of rows. Pushing projections down reduces row width. Avoiding Cartesian products often reduces work. These are useful heuristics for choosing candidates, not guarantees of the fastest plan. An expensive CPU-bound filter, available indexes, and the cost of materializing temporary results can all change the comparison.

For equality predicates A=B and B=C, transitivity allows us to add A=C. This inferred predicate may enable additional join orders while preserving the result. At the physical level, an equijoin might use block nested loops, index nested loops, sort-merge, or hashing. Data may be accessed through a scan or an index. Before choosing, check whether the index has the right key, whether an input is already ordered, and whether the smaller input fits in RAM.

Key takeaway

Inner-join reordering rules do not automatically apply to outer joins. Outer joins also preserve unmatched rows. Moving a join or a filter can remove rows that should have been retained.

Related source material: PDF pages 4–7. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Exercise: repair an invalid rewrite
sections.html:
Let R(a,x), S(a,b), and T(b,y) be joined using R.a=S.a and S.b=T.b. Someone rewrites (R join S) join T as R join (S join T), then removes R.a=S.a. Are the two plans still equivalent?

Show the solution

No. Changing the grouping of joins does not permit removing a join condition. The S join T subtree uses S.b=T.b; the top-level join must still check R.a=S.a. If S is projected early, both a and b must remain. List the columns available at each node before moving a predicate.

Related source material: PDF pages 4–6. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

quiz.question: Which columns must projection pushdown retain?
options: Only the columns in the final SELECT list
Output columns and every column still needed by later operators
quiz.explanation: Join keys and filter columns remain necessary even when they are absent from the final SELECT list.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes the parser, rewriter, and cost-based optimizer; query blocks and the System R approach; logical equivalences and safe simplifications; join reordering, cross products, and transitive predicates; selection and projection pushdown; and physical implementation choices. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
